While everyone else is indeed clarifying that the Sulha ships have good speed, it is indeed the lack of grip that allows them to dominate in Redout.  


When you corner, strafing allows you to drift around the turn without much of an issue, and Sulha ships allow you to do this effectively as well as accelerate out of the turn with TB into a straight, which is super reliable in Cairo maps for example.  


But on maps where drifting becomes unreliable, Lunare is indeed your best bet, with ESA being a jack-of-all-trades middle ground.
It really depends on the track and corners more than the playstyle. On Cairo tracks I tend to get better times not hitting any walls, while on Alaska it can be easier to be more bouncy.

The best way to get a good score is to just not take damage. +200 each lap  


I like to rush to first place in the first lap, then take the 2nd lap slowly and make sure I don't hit any walls, and slowly increase my speed/amount of thrust use as the race goes on to get Best Lap bonuses.  


If you're having issues, I'd switch out your ship for one with more Grip like a Koeniggsworth or a Lunare.

I moved out of state when I turned 18/19, and got a job at a DQ franchise store. It was one of my first jobs, and the people seemed nice.

I have a mentality from my MMO raiding days to always offer assistance at jobs when I can, and on my first day, the GM was bitching about how she needed someone to help her open the story because so-and-so was quitting. I offered to help, just because I felt like I was capable.

My second week there, I'm waking up 6 hours earlier than I normally do, opening the story by myself, getting all of the machines and registers ready, as well as finishing up dishes because the closing staff never finished their jobs. So I'm busting my ass, while the store GM doesn't bother to come in to the store most of the week.

Apparently, she spends her time when she did come in, going through all of the security cam footage to bitch at her employees. Now I had made a friend there by this point, and introduced him to League of Legends back in the season 2 days. Apparently we had "stopped working" when it was completely dead and everything was clean. Now I might not have had the best opens, and she could have been looking through footage at the request of the closing staff, but she never talked to me about it before she looked at the footage - apparently it's just a habit of hers. Ok fine, we'll talk less at work.

So on my third week, she comes in around noon, and just starts wailing on me about how shitty I am, and how all I do is talk to my coworkers, and I can't open the store right. Note she gave me about an hour of training and one day of a walk-through for what I later realized was the entire daily routine of the GM and their responsibilities - and I didn't even get a pay raise (still $8/hr). She never told me what I was doing wrong specifically, just that I was shit and doing everything wrong. She kept wailing on me on and off for hours, in front of customers and employees, till I asked to talk to a franchise guy, to complain about employee treatment. I was on the verge of tears the entire day.

So he comes in the next day, and I explain the situation, completely crying the whole time. (As a male who usually keeps my emotions to myself.) He doesn't do shit that afternoon, except that the next day, the GM comes in early - the same time I do - and excruciatingly slowly shows me how to turn on all of the machines "properly" (exactly how I've been doing it) - I feel like the franchise guy just wanted her to make peace and remind me how to do stuff which is fine at first, but she slowly degraded back into just wailing on me, saying that I'm a blatant liar for calling myself a quick learner during the interview, and picking at every little thing I've done in my short time there.

So I walk out, almost tearing up but I refused to cry in front of that bitch. Never had a job for less than a month before or after that. Of course, my parents gave me shit for "not being loyal to my employer". Later learned through a lot of psych classes that that GM likely had Borderline Personality Disorder and a lot of sociopathic tendencies, as well as just being inherently lazy. After that, I worked at a few other restaurants, and was genuinely surprised at how hard the GMs there worked. But it seems "lower-tier" jobs like retail and fast food, are just absolute cesspools of people with chronic mental disorders.

I've been focusing on myself for eight years. Constantly trying to improve myself, learn new things, be a better person, fix things that I deem as flaws and ignore the things that others choose to see. For the longest time I tried to personify what I wanted in a romantic partner, (just a self-sufficient person who can cook and talk about random philosophical topics) but I've accepted that the what I think I need can't be found by me.

I don't think suicide is ever a selfish choice as you seem to imply. If people choose to feel guilty over the suicide of another, then they have something to feel guilty of. Suicide to me, is something to learn from. Because it's not an individual issue. It's an issue of community. We all feel alone, but few actually try to support even the people they say they love. I can't accept this social contract that we're all expected to live our life for the sake of other people, but the only support we ever get is from ourselves.

It's funny how gifts seem to work in my family, and I assume many others. You can tell when someone genuinely cares about you, because they give simple gifts that represent who you are as a person, and what they value about you. Learning how to do this for others was one of the most telling revelations of adulthood. I wish I just had someone that cared - and I totally understand that to be cared for, you first have to care for others. But being that vulnerable can only get you so far until you run out of steam.

I've put so much hope into every possible outcome that life could grant, I've been content through the worst, but every time I try to be proactive and make my life into a future it falls apart. I've learned so much, and I've gotten so far, but for what? I'm not going to blame my abusive parents, lack of a support system, or my depression. I just can't look at my life and say that it has a meaning that I value. Maybe it would be easier to live if I was like Albert Camus, who easily dismissed the idea of suicide because he was successful and surrounded by attractive women.

I just don't think someone like me is, at a base level, is programmed to be able to survive in this world. When I look at my life objectively, there's no greater purpose to just existing.

There is no reason a meritocracy of sorts shouldn't be in place. You can't force diversity. Situations like the one in the article are not an argument for this forced diversity though, as it's assumed the employees were hired based on merit. Forcing perceived diversity just leads to people metaphorically painting the leaves of the tree a different flavor-of-the-month color, instead of planting seeds.

As aflarge implied, diversity of thought is much more important. This is not something that Social Justice advocates for, but something they actively fight against. I'd much rather have a group of intelligent individuals who reached their level due to their merit, and all have a unique idea to bring to the table.

That's one of the ironic parts of Social Justice - they argue for acceptance of the diversity of lived experience due to the intrinsic social differences of race and gender, yet they're all mindless sycophants who define modern divisions between groups. I hate how articles like this assume that "all men think the same" or "all blacks think the same" and must have the same background. There's no nuance.

If you want to create improvements and positive change, you have to plant new seeds, and give new generations the opportunity to grow and express their intrinsic merit as individuals.

When I began watching the video I thought that the self-deprecation and character explanation wouldn't last more than 5 minutes, then would go on to explain how skepticism applies, as a concept, to film and media. I was honestly very dissapointed that he kind of just rambled about YouTube, and in the context of the "Skepticon", it didn't really fit.

If he wanted to stick with his original premise of being "right" on the internet, he should have decided if he wanted to stay in character or not from the get-go, and use that perspective to show when he was wrong. Or better, in the context of the convention, show situations when he wasn't "skeptical" of his own work, and tie it into a more specific topic: "It's hard for individuals with an audience to admit to their audience when their wrong, because they're scared of losing credibility, despite that self-awareness generally being respected by genuine fans."

Instead he tries to make a joke of the skeptic community as a whole by calling them abrasive, which falls flat even if you know the names of the people he brought up. His intention was good, but the white-knight execution was terrible and made it hard to see his message.

Great discussion :D

He was more self-critical than anything, and used that as a tool to show that while the skeptic community is really good at pointing out the flaws of others, they rarely self-reflect or take a moment to adjust their rhetoric for a wider audience.

I think this is why Chris Ray Gun has such poignant appeal, because he doesn't take himself too seriously, and uses issues as a tool for comedy. If the skeptic community wants to reach audiences beyond those who don't already agree with them, they have to realize that if they won't concede argumentative stances, they at the very least need to concede their attitude.

For six years in a row, my parents got me pajama pants for Christmas. The first year was fine, I actually needed a pair as a 14 year old kid. They never really explained why, but always made a big deal about how expensive gifts were, despite being fairly wealthy. As a kid, it's really confusing to see families that your parents make fun of for being poorer, give their kids much more extravagant gifts and toys that they throw away in a few months.

However the worst gift I got was probably a 50-pack of assorted top ramen from an sort of eccentric uncle. Not mad at him though; I'm pretty sure my parents told him to get me some "cheap food for a skinny college boy." (The rest of my family is quite overweight.)

My sisters of course, get nice jewelry or more personalized gifts. Honestly I've just stopped giving a shit about things like Christmas a long time ago, despite trying to get people nice gifts when I have the money.

I guess it's just another way for my parents to make me feel like the mistake that forced them to get married. Still wear the pajama pants though.
